newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Citibank sees Greater China as Asia's bright spot.
newsitem.headline: Citibank sees Greater China as Asia's bright spot.

text.p: The economic outlook for Greater China is among the rosiest in Asia, Jason Kwok, chief economist for Citicorp unit Citibank North Asia, said on Thursday.

"The only economies in the region which have just come out from the bottom of their economic cycles and have begun to accelerate are China, Hong Kong and Taiwan," Kwok told a meeting of Citibank customers in Hong Kong.
He noted that the Philippines is nearing the top of its current economic cycle, while Indonesia and Malaysia have just passed the peaks of their cycles and have begun to slow down.
Thailand, South Korea and Singapore will continue to slow down and will soon hit the bottom of their economic cycles.
Citibank expects growth in China to rise to 10.3 percent in 1997 from an estimated 9.8 percent in 1996. Inflation should rise to 7.0 percent, up from an estimated 6.2 percent in 1996.
"Despite faster economic growth, inflation is not likely to increase substantially given the central bank's prudently tight monetary policy," said Kwok.
China will refrain from across-the-board easing this year on fears of spurring a surge in inflation, Kwok predicted.

"The cuts in interest rates in May and August last year, and any possible further cuts in interest rates in the near future, are simply attempts made by the government to ease the interest burden of the state-owned enterprises and to improve the profitability of banks," he said.
China's foreign exchange reserves, which already exceed US$100 billion, will rise on the back of a bigger trade surplus and continued foreign direct investment.

Hong Kong's economy will recover from a consumer spending slump that began in 1995, aided by improved political sentiment ahead of the handover to China on July 1, a fall in unemployment below 3.0 percent and a re-surge in property prices.
Hong Kong's growth will accelerate to 5.4 percent in 1997 from an estimated 4.8 percent gain in 1996. Inflation will rise to 7.2 percent this year from an estimated 6.0 percent in 1996.
Taiwan grew an estimated 5.6 percent in 1996, its poorest performance since a 7.6 percent rise in 1991, Kwok noted.

But he said growth should pick up in 1997 to 5.9 percent, led by increases in consumption and investment fueled by an improved political climate and loose monetary policy. Inflation will be 3.5 percent versus 3.1 percent in 1996, he said.
Taiwan's external financial position should recover from the setbacks experienced in the wake of tensions across the Taiwan Staits in March of last year, Kwok said.
Faster world growth and a cyclical recovery of the global computer market also will boost the growth of Taiwan's exports.

Kwok noted that because of the growing dependence of Taiwan's economy on China, the outlook for Taiwan in 1997 and beyond "will also very much depend on future development of the island's economic relations with China."
